It was long. The room was crowded.
The questions were difficult, but it was useful.
I was tired at the end.

Paula, I read the claim from Santos. Warehouse 4. Tell me what happened, and I don't want only the numbers.
Of course. The fire started at six fifty-five on Tuesday morning, near the old machine.
And before that? What was the team doing at that time?
They were working normally. Two men were loading a truck at door two, and three women were checking boxes near the office. Nobody was using the old machine.
Good. That is the line the reinsurer will read first. And the night manager?
He was closing his report in the office when he heard a noise. He was walking to door three when the fire started.
So he saw it start. Was anybody hurt?
No. The alarm rang and everybody left in four minutes. And while the team was leaving, one driver was moving his truck away from door two.
That driver saved us a truck. Paula, do you know why I asked you for the story and not for the numbers?
Because the numbers say how much, and the story says why?
Exactly. Anyone can send me a number. Send me the story and I can defend the claim in Miami. Keep writing them like this.
What were you doing when it happened?
The team was working normally. Nobody was hurt.
The fire damaged half of the warehouse.
We opened the claim this morning.

Hi, Paula. David here. Greg told me you sent the Santos report, and I want to tell you why he called you about it. Twelve years ago I was working on my first big claim. A fire in a factory, at night. I sent Miami a perfect page. The numbers were correct, the photos were good, and the dates were right. And Miami said no. They did not pay for four months. Four months, Paula. Do you know what was missing? Nobody wrote what the team was doing when the fire started. Nothing. Not one line. So the reinsurer read my page and they asked, was somebody working with fire that night? Was somebody using the old machine? And I could not answer, because I did not ask. The people were there, the answer was there, and I only asked three weeks later. By then, nobody remembered. So here is the thing I learned, and it is the only thing I really want you to keep from this call. In this job, what happened is easy. Anybody can write what happened. What was happening is the hard part, and it is the part that pays the claim.

Good morning, Paula. Sofia here, and I am going to be quick, because I only want to say one thing. This week you did something for the first time, and I do not think you noticed. Greg called you directly about the Santos fire. Not me. You. And you answered him in English, alone, about an international account, at seven in the morning. Two years ago you were sending me the reports and I was talking to Miami. Now you are talking to Miami. That happened this week, and nobody made an announcement. Now, about the grammar you learned today. I want you to see why it is not small. In our job there are two questions, and they are not the same question. What happened? A fire started at six fifty-five. Anybody can find that. But what was happening? Twelve people were working, two men were loading a truck, three women were checking boxes, and nobody was using the old machine. That second answer is the one the reinsurer reads first, and it is the one that decides if the client is paid. It is a small piece of English and it carries an enormous amount of money. So keep asking it, Paula. Every single time. What were you doing when it happened? See you Thursday.
